whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the B2C Commerce Architect exam?

personas.label: Experienced B2C Commerce architects
personas.description: You have led storefront projects and want to show that you can plan a complete commerce solution, not only build individual features.

personas.label: Commerce technical leads
personas.description: You choose between SFRA and a headless storefront, then plan integrations, caching, and site operations.

personas.label: Retail solution architects
personas.description: You design retail systems where B2C Commerce must work with Order Management, Marketing Cloud, and external services.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the B2C Commerce Architect exam?
examDifficulty.summary: This is a demanding commerce exam. You need strong B2C Commerce knowledge and must compare design choices, such as launch speed versus flexibility and custom code versus standard features. Salesforce lists B2C Commerce Developer as a prerequisite.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
65% to pass, which is 39 correct answers out of 60.
Questions ask you to choose a design. Be ready to compare SFRA and headless storefronts, OCAPI and SCAPI, caching options, and integration patterns.
Project experience helps. Work on real storefronts with different traffic levels and site setups is valuable preparation.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Experience launching a site and supporting it through busy trading periods is useful. Before booking, aim for at least 75% on practice tests and be able to explain when a headless storefront is a good fit.

examFormat.heading: What to expect on the B2C Commerce Architect exam
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test center. Expect questions like these:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe a retailer, such as a company with several brands and countries. You may need to choose how to organize sites, catalogs, code, or integrations.
bestWayToPass: Trace the cartridge path: Cartridges farther left take priority over those to the right. Put custom work in your own cartridge instead of changing the base.
Plan caching: Page caching is a major way to improve speed. Know which content can be cached and which shopper-specific parts must stay current.
Choose the right APIs: Learn SCAPI and Shopper APIs for newer headless builds, OCAPI for existing integrations, and SLAS for shopper sign-in.
Design for multiple sites: A shared master catalog can support separate storefront catalogs, price books, and locales for each site.

certificationCard.description: Show that you can plan and operate Salesforce B2C Commerce storefronts: choose a storefront model, organize sites and catalogs, design integrations, and protect performance and security.

keyConcepts.h2: B2C Commerce Architect exam: core ideas

blocks.heading: Architecture Patterns & Scalability
blocks.body: A B2C Commerce realm contains environments such as developer sandboxes, Development, Staging, and Production. Teams prepare and test code and data in Staging, then **replicate** them to Production. One realm can host multiple sites. Those sites may share code while using different catalogs, prices, and settings. For several brands or countries, a common design uses one **master catalog** for the product set, a **storefront catalog** for the assortment shown on each site, and **price books** for market or currency prices. The platform supports scale, but efficient code still matters: avoid costly work on every page request and use jobs for bulk processing.

blocks.heading: Storefront Architecture & Headless Commerce
blocks.body: **SFRA** (Storefront Reference Architecture) renders pages on the server and provides standard storefront features. Extend it with your own cartridges instead of editing its base code. **Composable Storefront** (PWA Kit with Managed Runtime) is the headless choice: a React front end that uses B2C Commerce APIs. It gives the team more front-end control, but the team must build and operate more pieces. SFRA often suits projects that value a faster launch and built-in commerce features. Headless can fit a highly custom experience or a shared front end for several back ends.

blocks.heading: Integration Architecture: OCAPI, SCAPI & Connectors
blocks.body: **SCAPI** (Salesforce Commerce API), including the Shopper APIs, is the modern API set and a common starting point for new headless storefronts. **OCAPI** (Open Commerce API) remains in use on many established sites. **SLAS** provides shopper sign-in and tokens for headless storefronts. For external services, configure calls through the Business Manager **service framework** to set timeouts, logging, and circuit breakers. Use scheduled **jobs** to import large product or inventory files, often in XML or CSV. Payment, tax, and address integrations may use certified **LINK cartridges**.

blocks.heading: Performance, Caching & CDN Strategy
blocks.body: Page caching is one of the main tools for improving response time. Cache full pages or suitable page sections with the iscache tag. Keep personal content, such as a shopper’s mini cart, in a small uncached section that loads separately. Choose cache times carefully and clear cached content when product or site content changes. The **eCDN** serves images and other static files from locations closer to shoppers. Watch platform **quotas**, which limit resources such as objects or API calls in a request, and fix quota violations before a busy season. Test with traffic patterns that resemble real promotions.

blocks.heading: Security, Compliance & Site Operations
blocks.body: Do not store unprotected card numbers in B2C Commerce. Send card data to a payment provider through its cartridge and keep a token on the commerce side; this can reduce PCI scope. Use Business Manager roles to give each team only the access it needs. Follow privacy, consent, and cookie requirements in each market. For operations, move code through Staging before replication, schedule large jobs away from busy periods, and monitor logs with alerts. Prepare for peak events such as Black Friday, including a deployment freeze when appropriate.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the B2C Commerce Architect exam
scenarioTips.intro: Read each retailer scenario for its number of brands and markets, the front-end experience it needs, and expected traffic. Use those details to choose a design and explain the trade-offs.

blocks.heading: Sites, Catalogs & Markets
blocks.body: For multiple brands or countries, consider one realm with several sites, a shared master catalog, and storefront catalogs and price books that fit each market.

blocks.heading: Cartridge Design
blocks.body: Keep custom code in your own cartridges and place them before the base cartridge in the path so your code can extend standard behavior without changing the base.

blocks.heading: Page Speed
blocks.body: Cache reusable page content. Load shopper-specific content separately so it does not prevent the rest of the page from being cached.

blocks.heading: External Integrations
blocks.body: Use SCAPI for current headless storefront work, jobs for large imports, the service framework for external calls, and suitable LINK cartridges for providers.

blocks.heading: Access & Operations
blocks.body: Tokenize payment data with a provider, assign Business Manager roles by job need, follow local privacy rules, and plan deployments and monitoring before peak events.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After B2C Commerce Architect, many people move toward the wider architect credentials:

sampleQuestions.question: A retailer sells across three brands and five countries. Many products are shared, but each brand has a different assortment and each country has different prices. Which catalog model fits?
options: Master catalog, site catalogs, market price books
Put each market price in a custom product attribute
Create a separate master catalog for every site
Show the same storefront catalog on every site
sampleQuestions.explanation: A shared master catalog avoids copying common products. Each storefront catalog controls its site’s assortment, while price books hold market prices.
whyWrong: Custom attributes bypass the normal price book model and make price maintenance harder.
Separate master catalogs duplicate shared products and complicate updates.
A single storefront catalog cannot control a different assortment for each brand.

sampleQuestions.question: An SFRA team needs to change checkout behavior. Where should developers make the change?
options: In site preferences in Business Manager
In a custom cartridge placed before the base cartridge
In a cartridge placed after the base cartridge
Directly in app_storefront_base
sampleQuestions.explanation: A custom cartridge earlier in the path can override or extend base behavior while keeping the base cartridge unchanged.
whyWrong: Site preferences do not replace checkout implementation code.
A later cartridge does not take precedence over the base cartridge.
Changing the base cartridge makes future upgrades harder and is not the recommended extension pattern.

sampleQuestions.question: A retailer wants a highly customized, app-like storefront built by its React team. Which approach is the best fit?
options: Call OCAPI from ISML templates
Extend SFRA with a custom theme
Use Composable Storefront with the Commerce APIs
Use only Business Manager content slots
sampleQuestions.explanation: Composable Storefront uses a React front end with Commerce APIs, giving the team control over a custom storefront experience.
whyWrong: OCAPI calls in server-rendered ISML templates do not provide the requested React headless storefront.
SFRA can be customized, but it remains a server-rendered storefront rather than the headless approach requested.
Content slots help manage content but do not create a complete React storefront.

sampleQuestions.question: Category pages slow down during peak traffic. Each page also renders the shopper’s mini cart. What should the architect recommend?
options: Run the entire category page as a job
Disable page caching so the cart stays current
Add more product images
Cache shared pages; load the mini cart separately
sampleQuestions.explanation: Cache the reusable category page and load the shopper-specific cart separately. This protects page speed while keeping cart details current.
whyWrong: A page displayed to shoppers cannot be replaced by a background job.
Turning off page caching removes a useful performance benefit for shared category content.
More images would add work and would not address the cart’s effect on caching.

sampleQuestions.question: A new headless storefront needs shopper sign-in and tokens for calls to the Shopper APIs. Which service should it use?
options: Shopper Login and API Access Service (SLAS)
Business Manager employee accounts
A shared API key stored in the front end
Basic authentication on every shopper request
sampleQuestions.explanation: SLAS handles shopper login and token access for headless B2C Commerce storefronts.
whyWrong: Business Manager accounts are for administrators and staff, not shopper authentication.
A secret embedded in front-end code can be exposed and is not a shopper login solution.
Basic authentication on each request is not the intended shopper token flow.

sampleQuestions.question: A retailer wants to reduce PCI scope and avoid keeping card numbers in B2C Commerce. What design should it use?
options: Use a tokenizing provider LINK cartridge
Encrypt card numbers in a custom object
Email card details to the finance team
Keep the card number only in session data
sampleQuestions.explanation: A provider can receive payment details and return a token, so the commerce site does not need to retain the raw card number.
whyWrong: Encryption does not remove the risk and scope created by storing card numbers in the platform.
Email is not a secure payment data flow and leaves card details exposed.
Session storage still puts card data on the commerce platform.

sampleQuestions.question: A warehouse sends inventory updates for 500,000 products every hour. How should the team load the feed?
options: Make one OCAPI request for each product every hour
Update inventory during every shopper page view
Enter each update manually in Business Manager
Run a scheduled inventory import job
sampleQuestions.explanation: A scheduled job can process a large inventory feed in batches and is suited to regular imports.
whyWrong: Hundreds of thousands of individual calls create avoidable overhead for a bulk feed.
Page requests should not be responsible for importing warehouse data.
Manual updates are not practical at this scale or frequency.

sampleQuestions.question: The team tested code in Staging and is ready to release it to Production. How is it normally moved?
options: Upload it to Production directly from each developer sandbox
Replicate it from Staging to Production
Rebuild the storefront by hand in Production
Copy the files to Production over FTP
sampleQuestions.explanation: The team prepares and tests changes in Staging, then uses replication to move them to Production.
whyWrong: Direct uploads from individual sandboxes bypass the standard release path.
Manually rebuilding Production is not the normal controlled deployment process.
FTP file copying is not the standard B2C Commerce deployment method.

sampleQuestions.question: An external tax service sometimes stops responding and holds up checkout. What should the architect configure?
options: Run the tax request only in an overnight job
Use the service framework with a timeout and circuit breaker
Make a plain HTTP request with no timeout
Call the tax service directly from the shopper’s browser
sampleQuestions.explanation: The service framework supports controls such as timeouts and circuit breakers so an unresponsive provider does not hold requests indefinitely.
whyWrong: Checkout needs a tax result during the shopper’s purchase, so an overnight job does not meet the need.
Without a timeout, a stalled provider can keep checkout waiting.
A browser-side call exposes integration details and does not provide the server-side controls needed here.

sampleQuestions.question: A new site is being designed with a headless front end. Which API set should the team consider first?
options: SOAP web services
OCAPI for every new headless feature
SCAPI and the Shopper APIs
Direct database access
sampleQuestions.explanation: SCAPI and the Shopper APIs are the current commerce APIs commonly used for new headless storefronts.
whyWrong: SOAP is not the default API choice for this new headless design.
OCAPI remains in use, but SCAPI is the modern starting point for new headless work.
Direct database access is not an appropriate storefront integration pattern.

sampleQuestions.question: Before Black Friday, load testing shows that some pages exceed platform quotas. What should the team do?
options: Tell shoppers to visit outside peak hours
Ignore the findings because quotas apply only in sandboxes
Disable the eCDN
Find and fix the quota-heavy code before peak trading
sampleQuestions.explanation: Quota issues can affect Production. The team should correct the code and retest before the expected traffic surge.
whyWrong: Changing shopper visit times does not correct the platform issue.
Production quotas also matter, so ignoring the test results is unsafe.
Disabling the eCDN does not fix the code that exceeds quotas and may hurt delivery performance.

sampleQuestions.question: The merchandising team should manage promotions but must not change code or payment settings. How should access be limited?
options: Least-privilege Business Manager roles
Give every merchandiser Administrator access
Remove the promotions tools from Business Manager
Have the whole team share one login
sampleQuestions.explanation: Business Manager roles can grant the promotion functions the team needs without granting unrelated permissions.
whyWrong: Administrator access is broader than the stated need.
Removing the promotions tools would prevent the team from doing its assigned work.
Shared accounts weaken accountability and do not enforce individual permissions.

sampleQuestions.question: Shoppers in Asia report that product images load slowly, while the main site runs in Europe. What can help most?
options: Bundle all images inside the application cartridge
Serve the images and static files through eCDN
Turn off page caching
Increase the image dimensions
sampleQuestions.explanation: The eCDN can serve static assets from locations closer to shoppers, reducing the distance those files travel.
whyWrong: Bundling images in the cartridge does not place them closer to shoppers and can complicate updates.
Page caching does not solve the geographic delivery of image files.
Larger images require more data and can make loading slower.

sampleQuestions.question: When is SFRA a better choice than a headless storefront?
options: When the site will not use any Salesforce APIs
When the team wants a React front end with full control
When the project values a fast launch and standard commerce features
When the same front end must serve a mobile app and store kiosks
sampleQuestions.explanation: SFRA provides standard storefront behavior and can help a team launch sooner when those features meet the requirements.
whyWrong: SFRA sites still use Salesforce platform capabilities and APIs as needed.
A React team seeking full front-end control is a stronger match for a headless storefront.
A shared front end across apps and kiosks may favor a headless architecture.

sampleQuestions.question: A retailer needs different home page banners by country, with changes managed by merchandisers and no code release. What should it use?
options: Hard-code banner content in ISML templates
Create separate cartridges for each country’s banners
Manage content slots and assets in Business Manager
Store raw HTML in a custom object
sampleQuestions.explanation: Business Manager content slots and assets let merchandisers manage site or locale content without changing code.
whyWrong: Hard-coded templates require a code change and deployment to update banners.
Country-specific cartridges add code and deployment work for content changes.
Raw HTML in custom objects is not the standard content-management approach.
